1.definition: Although the Byzantine Empire was the direct eastern continuation of the Roman Empire and its people called themselves Romans, their everyday and administrative language was Greek, not Latin. "Greek-speaking" marks that linguistic reality: a Roman state that thought in Greek.
The Rhos — the name Byzantine and Arab writers gave the Norse-led Rus’ traders and raiders, the people from whom “Rus’” and “Russia” take their name.

2.definition: Of Denmark or the Danes, the North Germanic people of the Jutland peninsula and surrounding islands. In the Viking Age the Danes were among the most active Scandinavian seafarers raiding and settling the North Sea coasts.

An early Latin and Greek rendering of "Rus'" — the name outside observers (here a Frankish chronicle echoing a Byzantine report) used for the Scandinavian traders and warriors operating along the eastern rivers, who turned out, on Frankish inquiry, to be Swedes.

3.term: Mother of cities of the Rus'
3.matchText: the mother of cities of the Rus
3.definition: The title Prince Oleg gave Kyiv when he seized it around 882, declaring it the senior city above all others — the political and ceremonial heart of the Rus' lands strung along the river routes.

The winter tribute circuit of the Rus': the prince and his war-band rode from one subject settlement to the next collecting furs, honey, wax, and slaves, then shipped the haul down the Dnieper to sell in Constantinople come spring.

A fortune-teller — someone believed able to foretell what is coming, by reading omens, casting lots, or sheer prophetic gift. In the Rus' chronicles a soothsayer is the figure who warns a prince how he will die, and is then proven grimly right.

The Old Norse personal name that the Slavs reshaped into "Oleg." It carries the sense of "holy" or "blessed," and its survival in the early Rus' dynasty is a small clue that those first rulers were still Norse-named even as they governed Slavic-speaking subjects.

4.definition: The leader of the Drevlians, a Slavic tribe east of Kyiv. After Prince Igor was killed extorting them for extra tribute, Mal proposed marrying Igor's widow Olga — a gambit she answered with a famously brutal revenge.

5.definition: The Old Norse personal name that the Slavic chronicles rendered as "Oleg" — one of the founding dynasty's Norse names, sitting beside Ingvar (Igor) and Helga (Olga) before the ruling house switched to naming its children in Slavic.

6.definition: A son of Svyatoslav set over the Drevlian land; not Oleg the Wise the regent of Chapter 3. He was killed in a rout during the war among the brothers and his body found in a ditch under the fallen.

Of or belonging to Norway, the Scandinavian kingdom on the western edge of the peninsula. The exiled claimant meant here is Harald Hardrada, who ran the Norway–Rus'–Constantinople circuit before winning the Norwegian crown.

8.definition: The Old East Slavic principle agreed at the 1097 Lyubech council — "let each hold his own patrimony." It conceded that each branch of the dynasty would keep its territory hereditarily, passing it down its own line rather than circulating it around the rota's shared ladder, and so ratified the very breakup the council met to prevent.

10.definition: Russian for "double faith": the long stretch after Rus' converted in 988 when people were officially Christian but still kept the old Slavic pagan habits — house-spirits, sky-god festivals, charms — folded quietly into the new religion rather than dropped.

11.matchText: the great Islamic empire of Khwarazm
